sections.history: Thirukachur lies in the low hills south-west of Chennai, near Singaperumal Koil, among the older living shrines of the Thondai country. Its Tamil name is read from Kachchapa, the word for tortoise, and the town is remembered as Alakkoil in the devotional tradition, a Paadal Petra Sthalam sung by the Tevaram saints. Two currents meet in its fame. In the first, Vishnu in his tortoise incarnation is said to have worshipped Shiva here to gain the strength to bear the churning mountain, and from this the Lord is named Kachabeswarar. In the second, and the one the town holds dearest, the saint Sundarar came hungry to the shrine, and the Lord himself went begging door to door to feed him. Founded in stone by the Cholas and enlarged under the later patrons of the Tamil country, the temple has been kept in continuous worship across the centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple stands within concentric rectangular enclosures of granite, its shrines ranged behind strong walls in the plain, enduring manner of the region. The sanctum holds the Shiva linga as Kachabeswarar, and the goddess Anjanakshi is honoured in her own shrine within the complex. Beside the temple tank, the Kurma Theertham named for Vishnu's tortoise form, stands a pillared hall remembered as the place where the hungry Sundarar rested and was fed, its stone pillars carved with care. Above the town a hill shrine, the Alakkoil from which the sthala takes its hymned name, looks down over the plain, and the twin shrine of Marundeeswarar is honoured in the same village, so that the pilgrimage here has long been made to more than one sanctuary.
sections.legends: Two legends hold Thirukachur. In the first, when the gods and asuras churned the ocean of milk, Vishnu took the form of the tortoise, Kurma, to bear Mount Mandara on his back; to gain the strength for it he worshipped Shiva at this place, and the Lord took the name Kachabeswarar, the master of the tortoise. The second is the story the town loves most. The saint Sundarar, journeying through, worshipped at the shrine and then lay down in the hall by the tank, faint with hunger. Shiva himself, as an old Brahmin, went from house to house through the village gathering alms, and came and served the saint a full meal, telling him the food had been begged door to door. When Sundarar rose to wash his hands the figure had vanished, and the Lord was known from then as Virundhitta Nathar, he who set out the feast.
sections.festivals: The temple's principal festival is the Brahmotsavam held in the Tamil month of Masi or Magam, in February or March, when the deities are drawn in procession through the town. A second Brahmotsavam and the full-moon Chitra Pournami are kept in Chithirai, in April or May. Maha Shivaratri, the great night of Shiva, and the monthly Pradosham are observed with devotion, as at every Shiva temple, and the memory of the Lord who fed the saint gives the offering of food a special place here. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Thirukachur rewards a reflective visit. Come to the sanctum of Kachabeswarar, then to the goddess Anjanakshi in her shrine, and walk out to the Kurma Theertham and the pillared hall beside it, where the story of the Lord who begged a meal for his hungry devotee feels near at hand. Many pilgrims climb to the hill shrine of Alakkoil for its wide view over the Thondai plain, and join the two sanctuaries of the village in a single round of worship. Though the Chennai–Chengalpattu road and railway pass close by, the temple keeps within its walls the quiet of a very old place.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from the evening into the night, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thirukachur lies near Singaperumal Koil on the Chennai–Chengalpattu road, about 2 km from Singaperumal Koil railway station on the Chennai Egmore–Chengalpattu line. Frequent suburban trains and buses serve Singaperumal Koil, and the temple is a short ride from the station; Chennai, with the nearest airport, is around 50 km to the north.
